title: Bad Affordable Housing Policy Contributes to the High Rate of Homelessness for Black Men
author: Algernon Austin
content:
The policy brief, “[Make Housing More
Affordable](https://cepr.net/publications/make-housing-more-affordable/),”
part of CEPR’s[ Majority Agenda](https://cepr.net/publications/the-majority-
agenda-good-jobs-strong-infrastructure-fair-play/), points out that “federal
housing policy directs too much funding to the wealthy and too little for
everyone else.” [For instance, ](https://cepr.net/publications/make-housing-
more-affordable/)most of the benefit of the mortgage interest deduction goes
to households with incomes over $200,000, and this policy costs the government
more than twice as much as the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit. Also, [only a
quarter](https://www.jchs.harvard.edu/sites/default/files/reports/files/Harvard_JCHS_Americas_Rental_Housing_2026.pdf)
of renters eligible for housing assistance receive it, [and less than 10
percent](https://endhomelessness.org/resources/top-5-immediate-takeaways-from-
huds-primary-annual-report-on-homelessness) of unhoused people are provided
housing by homelessness programs.

Prioritizing the wealthy has contributed to a high rate of homelessness which
disproportionately harms Black and Hispanic
people.[1](https://cepr.net/publications/bad-affordable-housing-policy-
contributes-to-the-high-rate-of-homelessness-for-black-men/#fn1) Although the
Black population makes up 12 percent of the overall population, they made up
30 percent of the homeless population in
2024.[2](https://cepr.net/publications/bad-affordable-housing-policy-
contributes-to-the-high-rate-of-homelessness-for-black-men/#fn2) The Hispanic
population makes up 20 percent of the US population but made up 31 percent of
the homeless.[3](https://cepr.net/publications/bad-affordable-housing-policy-
contributes-to-the-high-rate-of-homelessness-for-black-men/#fn3)

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/Screenshot-2026-08-12-at-9.08.21-AM-680x596.png)

Men were homeless at a higher rate than women (27 versus 18 per 10,000) in
2024.[4](https://cepr.net/publications/bad-affordable-housing-policy-
contributes-to-the-high-rate-of-homelessness-for-black-men/#fn4) Data by race
_and_ sex is not provided in the Department of Housing and Urban Development’s
__[_Annual Homelessness Assessment
Report_](https://www.huduser.gov/portal/sites/default/files/pdf/2024-AHAR-
Part-1.pdf) (AHAR).[5](https://cepr.net/publications/bad-affordable-housing-
policy-contributes-to-the-high-rate-of-homelessness-for-black-men/#fn5)
**Figure 2** shows a guesstimate made by applying the overall AHAR share of
men in the homeless population to the White and Black counts. Applying that
share yields a Black male homelessness rate of 71 per 10,000.

But it is not likely that Black men are merely as disadvantaged as men
overall. Black men are worse off than White men on many of the predictors for
homelessness (e.g., [low
income](https://www.mendeley.com/catalogue/0373301b-b6d4-3e3e-9da6-4feba924eaeb/),[
debt, and a history of
incarceration](https://academic.oup.com/jpubhealth/article-
abstract/40/1/65/3074503?redirectedFrom=fulltext)). A study of homelessness in
California by the University of California San Francisco (UCSF) from 2021 to
2022 found that[ 75 percent of the Black
people](https://homelessness.ucsf.edu/sites/default/files/2026-04/Black%20CA%20Report%202024.pdf)
experiencing homelessness were male. This is higher than the share of men –
[59.6
percent](https://www.huduser.gov/portal/sites/default/files/pdf/2024-AHAR-
Part-1.pdf)overall – in the AHAR data. Applying the UCSF share for Black men
yields a Black male homelessness rate of 89 per 10,000. This guesstimate is
likely to be closer to the real rate.

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/Screenshot-2026-08-12-at-9.11.37-AM-680x705.png)

Policy changes could drastically reduce or even eliminate homelessness. From
2009 to 2022, homelessness among veterans [declined by 55
percent](https://endhomelessness.org/state-of-homelessness/#report). This was
accomplished with [strategic](https://endhomelessness.org/state-of-
homelessness/#report)[ Housing First](https://endhomelessness.org/blog/how-
housing-first-ends-veteran-homelessness/) investments by the Department of
Veterans Affairs in collaboration with the Department of Housing and Urban
Development. [The National Alliance to End
Homelessness](https://endhomelessness.org/resources/top-5-immediate-takeaways-
from-huds-primary-annual-report-on-homelessness) observes:

> Congress could fund an end to homelessness nationwide. The estimated [9.6
> billion dollars](https://endhomelessness.org/resources/research-and-
> analysis/how-much-would-it-cost-to-provide-housing-first-to-all-households-
> staying-in-homeless-shelters/) required to house everyone living in a
> shelter during a given year is a small fraction of other federal programs.
> For example, _just over one percent of annual funding for the Department of
> Defense is enough to house every person experiencing homelessness._ But the
> Administration’s proposed cuts to homeless services along with recent
> changes to Medicaid, Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP),
> Supplemental Security Income and other supports will hurt response workers’
> efforts and make the crisis worse**.**

The Trump administration also [no longer
supports](https://endhomelessness.org/understanding-trumps-executive-order-on-
homelessness-attacks-on-housing-first/) the Housing First approach to address
homelessness even though it has been proven to be effective. It is important
to remember that the safety net cuts in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act were
done to help [pay for tax cuts to the
rich](https://www.cbpp.org/research/federal-tax/republican-megabill-trades-
essential-support-to-low-income-people-for-skewed). There would be much more
affordable housing if policymakers were to prioritize the needy over the rich.

**Notes.**

1) This discussion focuses on the rate of homelessness for Black people, but
the rates for American Indians and Alaska Natives (95 per 10,000) and for
Native Hawaiians and Pacific Islanders (186 per 10,000) are even higher. One
should also note that the Black homeless population is more than eight times
the size of the American Indian and Alaska Natives, and Native Hawaiians and
Pacific Islanders homeless populations combined.

2) Author’s calculations based on data from Tanya de Sousa and Meghan Henry,
The 2024 Annual Homelessness Assessment Report to Congress (U.S. Department of
Housing and Urban Development, 2024), Exhibit 1-7; and IPUMS USA, University
of Minnesota, www.ipums.org.

3) Ibid.

4) Ibid.
